summary: Defines a MIB for managing host computers, covering things like their storage, processes, and installed devices, so general-purpose hosts can be monitored in a uniform way. It was replaced by RFC 2790.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a dashboard for a computer, showing how full its disk is and what is running, so a manager can see its health from far away.

subtitle: A standard set of SNMP objects for watching a computer's storage, devices and software.

tldr.problem: SNMP could manage routers and similar gear, but there was no uniform set of objects for the common attributes of ordinary host computers.
tldr.mechanism: The Host Resources MIB defines six groups under host = { mib-2 25 }: system, storage, device, running software, running software performance and installed software.
tldr.outcome: It was a Proposed Standard and has been replaced by RFC 2790.

facts.label: Processor load
facts.value: 0 to 100, average over the last minute

today: RFC 1514 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2790, which is the version to use.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1514 defines a MIB for managing host systems. A host here means any computer that talks to other computers on the internet and is directly used by one or more people. The MIB covers attributes common to all such hosts, from personal computers to systems running Unix variants. It does not necessarily apply to devices whose main job is communications, such as terminal servers, routers and bridges, though that is not ruled out.

The objects are independent of the operating system, network services and software applications. Implementers of this MIB must also implement the System and Interfaces groups of MIB-II (RFC 1213).
sections.plainLanguage: This is a checklist of facts that every ordinary computer can report about itself, no matter which brand or system it uses.

sections.title: The Six Groups
sections.content:
Everything lives under host, which is { mib-2 25 }. Six groups sit beneath it: hrSystem, hrStorage, hrDevice, hrSWRun, hrSWRunPerf and hrSWInstalled.

The System, Storage and Device groups are mandatory for all host systems. The three software groups (running software, running software performance and installed software) are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The dashboard has six panels. Three show the basics and must be on every computer. Three show details about programs and are optional.

sections.title: Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module defines a few reusable types. Boolean is true(1) or false(2). KBytes is a memory size in units of 1024 bytes. ProductID is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER identifying the manufacturer, model and version of a hardware or software product, and the RFC suggests registering all of a manufacturer's products under one subtree so a station can work out the maker even for an unknown product. Unknown products use { 0 0 }.

DateAndTime is an octet string of 8 or 11 octets covering year, month, day, hour, minutes, seconds, deci-seconds and optionally the offset from UTC. If only local time is known, the time zone fields are omitted. InternationalDisplayString models text in some character set, most often NVT ASCII.
sections.plainLanguage: These are agreed ways to write things like sizes, dates and product names, so every computer says them the same way.

sections.title: System, Storage and Devices
sections.content:
The System group reports uptime since the host was last initialized (which differs from sysUpTime, the uptime of the management part), the local date and time, the device and parameters used to load the initial operating system, the number of user sessions, the number of processes and the maximum number of processes (zero if there is no fixed maximum).

The Storage group gives the size of physical main memory and a table of logical storage areas with a type (RAM, virtual memory, fixed disk, removable disk, floppy disk, compact disc, RAM disk or other), allocation unit size, size, amount used and a count of allocation failures. The RFC describes it as a diagnostic for "out of memory" and "out of buffers" failures and a way to track memory, disk or buffer usage.

The Device group has a table of all devices, each with a type, description, product ID, status and error count. Specific device types get their own tables: processors (with a load figure averaged over the last minute), network devices (mapped to ifIndex), printers, disk storage, partitions and file systems. A file system entry includes its mount point, remote mount point, type, access, whether it is bootable, the matching storage entry and the dates of the last full and partial backups.
sections.plainLanguage: These panels say how long the computer has been awake, how full each drawer of storage is, and what parts it has, such as disks, printers and processors, and whether each one is working.

sections.title: Running and Installed Software
sections.content:
The optional running software table has an entry for each distinct piece of software that is running or loaded in preparation to run, including the operating system, device drivers and applications. Each entry has a name, product ID, path, parameters, a type (operatingSystem, deviceDriver, application or unknown) and a status. Setting the status to invalid(4) causes the software to stop running and be unloaded.

The performance table adds, for each running entry, the centi-seconds of CPU used and the real memory allocated. The installed software table lists software stored locally, not software loaded from a network server, and is described as useful for inventory and for diagnosing version mismatch problems. Two timestamp objects let a manager see when the table last changed, so it can decide whether re-downloading is worthwhile.
sections.plainLanguage: One list shows which programs are running right now and how much of the computer each one is using. Another shows which programs are installed on the computer's own disks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Note that some objects are read-write, including the system date and the status of running software, where writing invalid unloads the software.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not talk about security, even though a few of the settings can be changed by a manager.

items.label: unknown
items.desc: The current state of the device is unknown.

items.label: running
items.desc: Up and running, no unusual error conditions known.

items.label: warning
items.desc: An unusual error condition was reported but the device is still operational.

items.label: testing
items.desc: Not available for use because it is being tested.

items.label: down
items.desc: The agent was told the device is not available for any use.
